So my family and I recently did a wine tasting in Italy, and later a nice steak dinner with some wine. I drank what I was told were some "very nice" wines (I've never experienced "bad" wines though, so idk), paired with some great-tasting food, but I can't really see why wine or other alcoholic drinks are great.

Well... that's not really true. I can see how wines really provide a nice compliment to whatever food you're drinking, have complex flavors that "evolve" over time, and come in those fun little glasses. And I guess these things are true of other drinks as well.

Really what I'm trying to say is that I don't really get why people drink alcohol:

  • It can impair your judgement, increasing the chance of you doing something stupid, and destroy your insides (though to be fair that's only in large amounts).

  • It seems to me like the taste of the alcohol itself at the end of the sip ruins whatever benefits you get from pairing the drink with another flavor.

I think it's kind of silly to intentionally drink a liquid that has been essentially been essentially just sitting in a container for months (years, even), being digested by a certain fermentation processes, has the potential to kill you in some form or another, as well as an overwhelming flavor at the end of a taste that doesn't really add anything to any meal, even considering the nicer flavors of the grapes/other ingredients.

To me, when I'm eating, say, steak or pizza or pasta or something, I can never imagine wanting to drink wine or beer with it instead of a cold can of Coke or Dr. Pepper (root beer for barbeque and ginger ale for seafood), or tea, because they don't have that huge bitter flavor. At least coffee, for its bitterness, has caffeine to wake you up. And for a standalone relaxation drink, I feel like nice, earthy tea (or soda) does a better job because it's good and warm.

Considering this, I feel like the role that alcoholic drinks play in societal interactions is really quite silly. So, what do you think about alcoholic stuff?
Do you drink? Why/why not? How much?

Wine and beer, they're enjoyable things. I like the taste of a cold moscatto and white wine is great, draught Guinness is brilliant. But I don't need these drinks, they're just extras in my day. I'm the type who can hold down a reasonable amount of the Devil's juice, and I don't go overboard with it (I'm afraid to let myself to).

I recently stopped drinking in solidarity with a friend who can't drink alcohol for his medical treatment, and I don't miss it. I still go out to pubs and do all the experiences usually in the drinking culture, and I don't think I'm missing out on too much. Usually when I would go out, I'd drink 3-4 pints or glasses, now I'm saving calories and money by not drinking when I go out.

Talk about destroying your insides, sods is so terrible for you.

As for alcohol, I believe the point is to get drunk, generally. All the stuff about food pairings and that is a bit tedious and I don't really get so sentimental about my food anyway (it's just something I need to live).

But being a bit drunk is quite nice. I think getting to like the taste is more of a pavlovian thing anyway. You associate the taste with the feeling, so therefore end up liking it.

It's sort of like how years ago, I was a heroin user. After a while, I got to the point where I just really liked the feeling of needles going in my vein. For a little while, after I quit I would even shoot water just to feel a needle prick. Now, like six years later, I still get a little excited when a needle comes out to get blood drawn or something. So I think liking the taste of straight alcohol is a bit like that. You get to like it over time because you like the feeling associated.

Unfortunately the 2nd Amendment didn't actually have anything to do with personal right to self defense, nor standing up against the government in the sense you seem to think it does (quite the opposite in fact). Your right to personal self defense would fall under the unenumerated rights referred to in the 9th Amendment, and your "right" to rebel against the government simply doesn't actually exist in the Constitution or related law, having been a minority view (held most famously by Jefferson for example) that was voted down by the majority who firmly believed in the need for a strong federal government and the power to put down such rebellions.

The founders were very clear that they were talking about a well regulated militia being necessary to protect against foreign invasion or domestic rebellion. The 2nd only deals with a restriction on the federal government, preventing them from disarming a specifically defined "well regulated militia" that serves those purposes. The "well regulated militia" (which was previously more fully defined in the Articles of Confederation, and expanded up on by Washington, Hamilton, etc) was defined in the Militia Acts of 1792, 1862, 1903, etc.

"No vessel of war shall be kept up in time of peace by any State, except such number only, as shall be deemed necessary by the United States in Congress assembled, for the defense of such State, or its trade; nor shall any body of forces be kept up by any State in time of peace, except such number only, as in the judgement of the United States in Congress assembled, shall be deemed requisite to garrison the forts necessary for the defense of such State; but every State shall always keep up a well-regulated and disciplined militia, sufficiently armed and accoutered, and shall provide and constantly have ready for use, in public stores, a due number of filed pieces and tents, and a proper quantity of arms, ammunition and camp equipage."

Further, regarding the Militia Acts;

The first Act, passed May 2, 1792, provided for the authority of the president to call out the militias of the several states, "whenever the United States shall be invaded, or be in imminent danger of invasion from any foreign nation or Indian tribe." The law also authorized the President to call the militias into Federal service "whenever the laws of the United States shall be opposed or the execution thereof obstructed, in any state, by combinations too powerful to be suppressed by the ordinary course of judicial proceedings, or by the powers vested in the marshals by this act". This provision likely referred to uprisings such as Shays' Rebellion. The president's authority in both cases was to expire after two years.

The second Act, passed May 8, 1792, provided for the organization of the state militias. It conscripted every "free able-bodied white male citizen" between the ages of 18 and 45 into a local militia company. (This was later expanded to all males, regardless of race, between the ages 18-54)

Militia members, referred to as "every citizen, so enrolled and notified," "...shall within six months thereafter, provide himself..." with a musket, bayonet and belt, two spare flints, a cartridge box with 24 bullets, and a knapsack. Men owning rifles were required to provide a powder horn, 1/4 pound of gunpowder, 20 rifle balls, a shooting pouch, and a knapsack. Some occupations were exempt, such as congressmen, stagecoach drivers, and ferryboatmen. Otherwise, men were required to report for training twice a year, usually in the Spring and Fall.

The militias were divided into "divisions, brigades, regiments, battalions, and companies" as the state legislatures would direct. The provisions of the first Act governing the calling up of the militia by the President in case of invasion or obstruction to law enforcement were continued in the second Act. Court martial proceedings were authorized by the statute against militia members who disobeyed orders.

This was an obligation to the state, not a right that you could choose whether or not you wished to exercise. And the 2nd served only to restrict the federal government from disarming a well regulated militia that was acting under that obligated and defined structure in the defense of the state.

This well regulated militia is further defined and constrained by the powers granted to the Congress and the President in the Constitution itself to take control of these well regulated militias in order to put down rebellions, following the examples set by Shay's Rebellion and the Whiskey Rebellion.

First, Congressional powers over the Militia, from Article 1 Section 8 of the Constitution.

"To make Rules for the Government and Regulation of the land and naval Forces; To provide for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions; To provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining, the Militia, and for governing such Part of them as may be employed in the Service of the United States, reserving to the States respectively, the Appointment of the Officers, and the Authority of training the Militia according to the discipline prescribed by Congress;"

Next, the Presidential powers over the Militia as defined in Article 2 Section 2 of the Constitution.

"The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and of the Militia of the several States, when called into the actual Service of the United States;"

Thus, the first 8 Amendments of the "Bill of Rights" serve to place restrictions upon federal power, and only reference so called "enumerated rights" in the context of placing restrictions on the federal government from infringing them. And in the case of the 2nd, the right in question is the right of a defined "well regulated militia" to not be disarmed by the federal government, as the militia is needed to protect the state from foreign invasions and local rebellions against the state government and law enforcement.

Again, the "right" to rebel against the government was rejected by the majority of the founders and was not included in the Constitution or accompanying body of law. Your personal right to self defense has nothing to do with the 2nd, and actually falls under the 9th's unenumerated rights already assumed and reserved by the people.

While the NRA has been very successful in their heavy lobbying campaign over the past few decades (since the 1970s) of convincing the judicial and legislative branches to overturn the historical facts and 200 years of correct and plain understanding of the 2nd Amendment, it doesn't change what the 2nd actually said, what the founders said it meant, the actual historical context, the explanations of the meaning by the founders themselves, in the Articles of Confederation, and in the Constitution, etc.

Shays‍ '​ Rebellion was an armed uprising in Massachusetts (mostly in and around Springfield) during 1786 and 1787. Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays led four thousand rebels (called Shaysites) in rising up against perceived economic injustices by Massachusetts, and in a later attempt to capture the United States' national weapons arsenal at the U.S. Armory at Springfield. Although Shays' Rebellion met with defeat militarily against a privately-raised militia, it prompted numerous national leaders (including George Washington, who came out of retirement to deal with issues raised by Shays' Rebellion) to call for a stronger national government to suppress future rebellions, resulting in the U.S. Constitutional Convention and according to historian Leonard L. Richards, "fundamentally altering the course of U.S. history."

Traditionally depicted as a revolt of poor farmers embittered by land seizures and bankruptcies, recent research into the lives of Shays Rebellion's participants suggests that Shaysites came from diverse socio-economic backgrounds, and from different professions and states. Research shows that the Shaysites' grievances extended beyond the specifics of Massachusetts' economic situation to issues like: rule by a faraway elite; cronyism and corruption in government; and regressive tax policy.
